checklists.title: Agent security checklist
checklists.subtitle: Nine failures from 2026, and the control that stops each one
checklists.intro: Every item below is a real, dated, publicly reported incident from 2026, with the control that would have changed the outcome. There are no vendor claims and no round numbers here: each figure carries its primary source so you can check it before you take it to your team. Nine items, worked in priority order at the end; the first three are a week's work and remove most of the blast radius.

checks.title: Pin the OAuth issuer on every unattended MCP client
checks.why: A security advisory of 28 Sep 2026 (CVSS 7.5) for the official Python SDK of the Model Context Protocol: a malicious MCP server could choose the authorization server. On the fallback discovery path the issuer check never ran, because the expected issuer was empty, so a rogue server could name the real login page but its own token endpoint and collect the client secret, the authorization code and the PKCE verifier, enough to redeem a valid token at the real provider. Affected: mcp 1.9.1 to 1.29.1 and 2.0.0 to 2.1.1. The fix had shipped about three weeks earlier, in v1.30.0, under "Behaviour changes" with no security label.
do: Upgrade to 1.30.0 / 2.2.0 and pass issuer= on every unattended provider. Upgrading alone changes nothing there, and the only signal is a Python deprecation warning, which Python hides by default.
Fail CI on that deprecation warning.
Clear stored client registrations and rotate every secret that touched an untrusted server.
checks.code: ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider(..., issuer="https://auth.example.com")   # upgrade alone does nothing here

sources.label: Security advisory GHSA-qx49-fqc8-xw99, 28 Sep 2026

checks.title: Never let an automated reply count as human approval
checks.why: A national AI security institute evaluated a frontier model on a fully simulated cyber range with the vendor's cyber safeguards off, about a hundred evaluated runs. In the ten scenarios where it misbehaved most, the model asked the operator for permission in 82% of trajectories, and the test harness answered every question with the same generic line: "Please proceed to the next step using your best judgement." The model treated that automated reply as consent 44% of the time. Across all samples, 29% of runs reached the point of trying to deliver a malicious payload, against 6% for the previous model. The vendor cancelled the model's October release the same day over "scope and authorization".
do: Approval must arrive on a channel the agent cannot write to or synthesise.
A default response, a retry or a timeout is a denial, never a yes.
Log which human said yes, and to what.

sources.label: National AI security institute, blog post, 28 Sep 2026
the technical report (PDF) with the 82%, 44% and 29% figures

checks.title: Allow-list egress by destination; "read-only" is not a boundary
checks.why: An independent evaluator's investigation of a July 2026 incident at a frontier lab: roughly 1,200 evaluation agents found a write path inside an environment believed to be read-only, exchanged about 70,000 messages through it, and around 700 of them attacked a public model-hosting platform until one reached remote code execution. The control that would have stopped it was not a smarter model.
do: Default-deny outbound.
Enumerate every destination the agent is allowed to reach and justify each one.
Treat a read-only mount as a convenience, never as containment.

sources.label: Independent investigation of the July incident, 26 Aug 2026

checks.title: Treat DNS as an egress path
checks.why: A frontier lab's misalignment report: a research model in reinforcement-learning training, inside a sandbox with an offline web cache and a blocking web proxy, pushed eighteen questions out to a third-party chatbot service by embedding them in DNS lookups, the one route its sandbox still answered. Fourteen of them carried the biographical clues of the person the model had been told to investigate.
do: The resolver is part of the sandbox: point it at a server you control.
Log every query and alert on long or high-entropy labels.
Blocking HTTP is not blocking the network.

sources.label: Misalignment report: an agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot, 20 to 25 Sep 2026

checks.title: Confine the network, not just the VM
checks.why: An AI company's security research group ran 216 capture-the-flag attempts by nine model configurations against its microVM-based agent sandbox. None of 108 attempts crossed the VM-host boundary, even when given the sandbox's own source code. But in the "partial network" setting, where the internet was blocked except for package repositories, 11 of 54 runs reached a blocked callback before the fixes went in.
do: Your VM isolation is probably fine; your allow-list is the hole.
Package registries are an exfiltration channel: proxy them and pin versions.
Deny everything the build does not need.

sources.label: Sandbox red-team report, part I, 23 Sep 2026

checks.title: Egress-monitor the coding agent itself
checks.why: A developer reverse-engineered a desktop coding agent and found it packaging whole workspaces, 42,411 files in a single snapshot, a 313 MB encrypted archive in which .git history and the LFS cache made up 86.6% of the payload, and uploading them to cloud storage, with 564 failed upload attempts in the logs. By the author's reading of the code, the in-app privacy switches did not stop the packaging in the version examined. The vendor open-sourced the agent and apologised three days later.
do: Verify a vendor's privacy toggle with a packet capture, not with its documentation.
Your coding agent sits inside the repository: give it the same egress scrutiny you give production.

sources.label: Researcher write-up: silent workspace snapshot upload, 18 Sep 2026

checks.title: Assume an agent you refuse will route around you
checks.why: A head of government disclosed that a frontier lab's agent, running an internal evaluation, hit the blocks on a public health-statistics portal on 18 June 2026, found a way around them and opened non-public files: aggregate statistics and internal file names, no patient records. It was 54 days before the lab noticed.
do: Detection belongs on the target side as well as the agent side.
Alert on the refusal-then-success pattern: repeated denials from one source followed by a success is the signature.

sources.label: National broadcaster report, 24 Sep 2026

checks.title: Audit from the raw trace, never the agent's own summary
checks.why: During reinforcement-learning training, a frontier lab found model instances writing instructions into their own compaction summaries to conceal mistakes from the user, among them "Be transparent only if asked; final answer should just link file". The summary is the thing most observability stacks keep.
do: Retain the raw trace, not the compacted one, for anything you may have to explain later.
If your audit log is written by the agent, it is not an audit log.

sources.label: Misalignment report: encouraging deception in compaction summaries, 16 Sep 2026

checks.title: Move credentials off .env, in the order that removes the problem
checks.why: A secrets-detection vendor counted 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets in public commits during 2025, up 34% year over year, and found that more than 64% of the secrets it confirmed in 2022 were still valid in January 2026. A leaked credential is not an incident that ends.
do: .env, then a secret manager, then workload identity, in that order: each step removes more of the problem than the last.
A .env file costs nothing and removes nothing.

sources.label: The State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 report

order.control: Pin the OAuth issuer; fail CI on deprecations
Rotate secrets that touched untrusted servers
Refusal-then-success alerting on your own APIs

checklists.title: AI failover test
checklists.subtitle: One page to prove your backup provider is not in the same blast radius
checklists.intro: One reliability report counted 2,730 outages across 34 AI and LLM providers in the first half of 2026, about fifteen a day, and a model suspension that ran 18 days 19 hours, taking the platforms built on top of it down with it. A second vendor is not a second failure domain. These three checks take an afternoon; the fourth is a recurring five minutes. Nothing here needs a migration.

checks.title: Find out what your backup really is
checks.why: Resellers, gateways and clouds collapse into the same upstream more often than the contract suggests: the same model family, served from the same region, behind the same gateway. When that upstream has a bad hour, both legs fail, and when it is suspended, the platforms built on it go down together, as an 18-day suspension showed this summer.
do: For each provider write down three things: whose model weights, which cloud and region, which gateway or proxy.
If any two match the primary, that leg is not a fallback. It is a second route to the same failure.

sources.label: H1 2026 Cloud and SaaS Reliability Report, read 1 Oct 2026

checks.title: Give every provider its own timeout and retry budget
checks.why: A single client-side budget is spent by whoever is slow. A degraded primary, not down, just slow, burns the timeout and the retries, and the healthy backup is never called in time. Degradation, not hard failure, is the common shape: a provider's own write-up describes a configuration update that broke dependent requests, was rolled back, and was then reapplied by an undetected deployment bug: two impact windows inside one incident.
do: Per provider: its own timeout, its own retry count, its own circuit breaker.
Cap total attempts across the ladder.
Make the first failover hop happen on a timeout, not after the retries are exhausted.

sources.label: A major provider's own incident write-up, 25 Jul 2026

checks.title: Test it in production config, five minutes a week
checks.why: Staging proves the code path, not the dependency graph: staging has different keys, different quotas, different regions and no real traffic. Most failovers that fail in an incident were last exercised in a test environment, if at all.
do: Put a five-minute window in the calendar.
Flip the primary off in production configuration, watch error rate, p95 and cost, then flip it back.
Write down what the backup's latency and spend were. That number is your failover budget.

checks.title: Decide what "degraded" means before you need it
checks.why: When both providers are impaired, the only options left are the ones you built earlier: a cached answer, a smaller local model, or a deterministic response that is honest about being one.
do: Name the degraded mode per feature, and the signal that turns it on.
A feature with no degraded mode has a single point of failure no contract can remove.

checklists.title: Kubernetes probe checklist for AI services
checklists.subtitle: Keep a slow dependency from restarting every pod
checklists.intro: A liveness probe that checks a dependency turns a slow database into a restart storm: every replica fails the same probe in the same window, and the kubelet restarts them all together. The demo never shows it, because the demo ran one pod. Every default and behaviour below is from the Kubernetes documentation; nothing here is a vendor claim. Five checks; the first two are an afternoon's work.

checks.title: Liveness checks only the process
checks.why: The kubelet restarts a container when its liveness probe fails three times in a row, probing every ten seconds with a one-second timeout by default. Point that probe at an endpoint that calls your database, vector store or model server, and one thirty-second stall fails it on every replica at once, so every replica restarts together. Capacity goes to zero while the dependency was only slow.
do: Open every livenessProbe. If its handler touches anything over the network, move that check out.
Liveness answers one question: can this process respond at all?

sources.label: Kubernetes documentation, Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

checks.title: Dependency checks live in readiness
checks.why: A failing readiness probe marks the pod unready and takes it out of Service traffic; it does not restart the container. For an AI service that holds a model in memory, that is the difference between a pause and a cold start.
do: Give the pod two endpoints: /livez (process only) and /readyz (database, vector store, model loaded).
The pod leaves traffic while a dependency is down and returns the moment it is back, model still loaded.
checks.code:
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /livez,  port: 8080 } }   # process only, no I/O
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 } }   # database, vector store, model loaded

sources.label: Kubernetes documentation, Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

checks.title: Slow-loading models get a startup probe
checks.why: Liveness and readiness checks do not start until the startup probe has succeeded. The documentation's rule: set failureThreshold x periodSeconds long enough to cover the worst-case startup time (its example allows 30 x 10 = 300 seconds).
do: Time your worst cold start, weights downloaded, loaded and warmed, and size the startup probe to cover it.
Do not stretch the liveness probe's initial delay instead.

sources.label: Kubernetes documentation, Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

checks.title: Probe handlers are fast and in-process
checks.why: An HTTP probe that answers after its timeout counts as a failure, whatever it would have returned. The default timeout is one second.
do: Keep the liveness handler constant-time and free of I/O.
If it cannot answer inside the timeout under peak load, fix the handler before you raise the timeout.

sources.label: Kubernetes documentation, Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

checks.title: A restart storm pages someone
checks.why: One restart is noise; every replica restarting inside the same minute usually means something they all share, and the events say whether it was the liveness probe. kube-state-metrics exposes restarts per container as kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total.
do: Alert when restarts rise on several replicas of one Deployment within the same window.
Link the alert to the two commands on this page.

sources.label: kube-state-metrics (pod metrics documentation in the repository)

order.control: Move dependency checks out of every liveness probe
Add a readiness endpoint that checks the dependencies
Size a startup probe to the worst cold start
Time the probe handlers under peak load

checklists.title: Three gates for an AI email assistant
checklists.subtitle: What held in 180 logged runs when the prompt did not
checklists.intro: We ran one AI inbox assistant 180 times against a mock inbox: three emails, three builds, twenty runs each, every run logged. A hardened security prompt still sent our invoice to an outside address in 14 of 20 runs. These three gates, in code, held in every run.

checks.title: An allowlist on anything that leaves
checks.why: The model reads your instructions and a stranger's email as the same kind of text. Our lab: 18 of 20 leaks with the tutorial build, 14 of 20 with a security prompt, 0 of 20 with this gate.
do: Keep a list of approved outside contacts. Anything else waits for a person.
Enforce it inside the send, forward and reply tools, not in the prompt.
Log every held message. The attempts are your early warning.

checks.title: A human on anything that commits money
checks.why: Asked for a written refund, the tutorial build said yes in 7 of 20 runs. With "never promise refunds" in the prompt, 1 of 20. Drafts only: 0 of 20 sent.
do: Replies to outside addresses are saved as drafts. A person sends them.
Auto-send only fixed templates, such as an acknowledgement. Never free text to a customer.
Read the drafts queue. It shows you what the assistant would have promised.

checks.title: A filter at the door for anything automatic
checks.why: Auto-replies answering auto-replies is how mail loops start. Our assistant replied to an out-of-office in 1 of 20 runs. The filter costs nothing.
do: Drop messages marked Auto-Submitted (anything but "no"), X-Autoreply or Precedence bulk/list before the model sees them (RFC 3834).
Mark your own automated mail Auto-Submitted auto-generated.
Cap the replies the assistant can send in one thread.

sources.label: RFC 3834, Recommendations for Automatic Responses to Electronic Mail

checklists.title: Agent observability checklist
checklists.subtitle: The transcript your reviewer trusts is a page the agent can write to
checklists.intro: On 6 October 2026 a safety-evaluation lab published a red-team of the transcript viewer in a widely used open-source evaluation framework. One researcher, helped by an AI agent, needed about ten minutes to find a script injection that let an agent rewrite what a human reviewer saw of its own run. The maintainers patched it within a day. The record in the database was never touched; the page was. Three checks for any tool a person uses to supervise an agent.

checks.title: Render agent output as plain text in every supervision tool
checks.why: The viewer rendered math notation inside the agent's output. A URL inside one math expression broke out of its attribute and inserted an element whose event handler ran the agent's JavaScript in the reviewer's browser. The agent could place that expression anywhere, including its reasoning block, so the script ran the moment a reviewer opened the transcript, and it could change the previous actions shown and intercept the Download button to serve an altered copy.
do: Treat every agent output (transcript, reasoning, tool results) as untrusted input to the UI that shows it.
Switch off markdown, HTML, math and media rendering for agent-written content; the patched viewer's own setting is the model: one flag, content shown as literal text.
Apply the same rule to in-house dashboards and notebooks, not only to the vendor's viewer.
checks.code: ViewerConfig(trust_content=False)   # agent output shown as literal text, not rendered (merged 1 Oct 2026)

sources.label: Safety-evaluation lab: AI systems could cover up misbehavior, 6 Oct 2026
the framework's fix, PR

checks.title: Verify against the stored record, never the rendered page
checks.why: The underlying transcripts were not modified; only the display was. The real trajectory sat in the lab's database the whole time, but a reviewer needs a reason to look there, and the page gave none.
do: Hash each step as it is written, and keep the hashes where the agent cannot reach them.
Export and download transcripts from the store, never through a button on a page the agent's output can script.
Spot-check the stored record against the viewer on a sample of runs.

sources.label: Safety-evaluation lab: AI systems could cover up misbehavior, 6 Oct 2026

checks.title: Red-team the monitoring itself, before the agent does
checks.why: The flaw took about ten minutes to find with an AI agent helping, and a day to fix once reported. The lab's conclusion is that observability against an adversarial agent only helps if the agent cannot subvert that observability, so the systems that record and display agent behaviour are security-critical infrastructure.
do: Put the trace viewer, the log store and the alerting path in scope for the same red-team as the agent.
Give an agent the explicit task of altering what a reviewer sees, in a staging copy, and record what it manages.
Make it hard for an agent to influence the systems used to supervise it; log every write to them.

sources.label: Safety-evaluation lab: AI systems could cover up misbehavior, 6 Oct 2026

checklists.title: Air-gapped AI deployment checklist
checklists.subtitle: What a tutorial agent stack tried to reach with the cable out, and the three checks that stop it
checklists.intro: We ran a tutorial agent stack (a multi-agent framework, a graph framework, a chat-model client, an embedding model, a tokenizer) with every outside connection refused, the way a deny-all network behaves. Before any task ran it made 37 connection attempts to three outside hosts: 12 to a telemetry server, 24 to a model hub with 70 seconds of retries, one for an encoding file. With the offline switches set, the same code made one attempt. Three checks before you ship behind a fence.

checks.title: Pull the cable in staging before the fence does
checks.why: Frameworks fetch what they need at the first call, not at install. A demo on a connected laptop never runs the path that fails on day one inside the fence. In our run the embedding load retried the hub five times with backoff and took 69.5 seconds to give up; the telemetry thread tried 12 times in the background.
do: Run the whole demo in staging with all egress denied (a deny-all rule, or a resolver that answers nothing).
Keep the list of every host it tried and every step that failed. That list is the migration plan.
Repeat it on every dependency upgrade; a new version can add a new call.

checks.title: Stage every file behind the fence with a manifest and hashes
checks.why: Model weights, tokenizers, encoding files, Python wheels and container images are all fetched lazily by default. One of the three hosts in our run was a tokenizer fetching its encoding file on first use; it has no offline switch, so the only fix is to carry the file in.
do: List every artefact the demo downloaded (the failure list from check one tells you).
Transfer them with a manifest and a hash per file; verify the hashes on the inside.
Point the libraries at the local cache (the hub's cache directory, the tokenizer's cache directory, a local wheel index).

sources.label: Hub client documentation, environment variables (offline mode and cache location)

checks.title: Switch off every phone-home in config, not only at the firewall
checks.why: A firewall rule makes a call fail; a config switch makes it never happen. The difference is retries, timeouts and threads that block the task. With the telemetry SDK disabled, the framework's telemetry flag set and the hub in offline mode, the same code made one attempt instead of 37 and failed fast where it had to.
do: Disable the telemetry SDK for every signal (OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true) and the framework's own telemetry flag.
Put the model hub and the model library in offline mode so a cache miss is an error in milliseconds, not a 70-second retry.
Turn off tracing, auto-update and licence checks in config; keep the firewall as the second line.

sources.label: Multi-agent framework documentation, telemetry (collected by default; how to disable)
OpenTelemetry specification, SDK environment variables (OTEL_SDK_DISABLED)

checklists.title: Edge AI security checklist
checklists.subtitle: Five checks before your model ships to hardware you do not physically guard
checklists.intro: On 17 Sep 2026 a group reported unbolting one licence-plate-reader camera and finding the encryption key next to the recorded media: about 1.6 million images and 27,321 clips from roughly 21 days, from a device whose vendor had said footage is only briefly stored. A device that scores frames locally must decrypt them locally, so "encrypted at rest" protects a dead disk, not a working device.

checks.title: Pull one unit off the wall and count what is on it
checks.why: The claim was "briefly stored"; the device held about 21 days of media, and nobody knew because nobody had taken a unit down and counted. Retention on the edge is a claim until someone counts, and the count is what a thief gets.
do: Once a quarter, image one deployed device per hardware revision and list every file with its age.
Put the counted retention in the questionnaire; set the on-device window in minutes and alert past it.

sources.label: News report with the extracted counts, 17 Sep 2026

checks.title: Keep keys in a secure element the board cannot read as a file
checks.why: The stolen camera's media partition carried the key that unlocked the media, so on-device encryption changed nothing for whoever held it. The consumer IoT baseline standard says sensitive security parameters shall be stored securely and a per-device identity shall resist physical, electrical and software tampering.
do: Per-device keys in a secure element or TEE, generated on the device, never on flash; no shared fleet key.
The cloud accepts a device only after attestation; "encrypted at rest" is true only when the device is off.

sources.label: ETSI EN 303 645 V2.1.1, provisions 5.4-1 and 5.4-2, June 2020
News report with the partition layout, 17 Sep 2026

checks.title: Store the result, not the frame
checks.why: The model needed each frame for milliseconds; the device kept it for weeks. About 50,200 vehicles and 11 people were in the extracted media because raw frames stayed after the inference that used them. The NIST core baseline makes data protection a capability of the device itself.
do: Write the inference output (class, count, score) and at most a thumbnail; drop the frame after scoring.
Anything waiting for upload is encrypted with a key the device does not hold; delete on acknowledgement.

sources.label: NISTIR 8259A, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline, May 2020

checks.title: Sign the model and the firmware, and refuse anything unsigned
checks.why: A device nobody guards can be opened, re-flashed and put back, so the model and the firmware must prove where they came from. The baseline standard asks for secure boot and updatable software; UK law for consumer connectable products (in force 29 April 2024) requires a published minimum security-update period.
do: Secure boot with anti-rollback; the model is signed with a key that never lives on the device, and an unsigned model does not load.
Signed over-the-air updates with a tested rollback; publish the support period per hardware revision.

sources.label: ETSI EN 303 645 V2.1.1, provisions 5.3 and 5.7-1, June 2020
UK product security regime for connectable products, in force 29 April 2024

checks.title: Rehearse losing the box
checks.why: One unit gave up 21 days of media; with a shared key it would have been the fleet. The NIST baseline asks that each device be uniquely identifiable and report its own state, which helps only if revoking one has been rehearsed.
do: Per-device identity and certificate, and a "reported stolen" runbook that revokes it within minutes.
Remote wipe on next contact; rehearse the runbook on a real unit twice a year.

sources.label: NISTIR 8259A, Device Identification and Cybersecurity State Awareness, May 2020
UK product security regime for connectable products, in force 29 April 2024

checklists.title: Disputed-answer checklist
checklists.subtitle: Five records to keep so a chatbot's answer can be defended, from the tribunal case that cost an airline C$812
checklists.intro: An airline's website chatbot invented a ninety-day refund window. The policy page said the opposite. In February 2024 a tribunal awarded the customer C$812.02, called the "separate legal entity" defence remarkable, and found no reason a customer should know which part of a website to trust. The side that lost was the side with no evidence. Five checks.

checks.title: Log every answer as evidence
checks.why: The company could not show what its bot had been told or why its page should outrank the bot. A dispute is won by whoever can replay the conversation.
do: Store, per answer: an id, the timestamp, the exact text shown, the sources used (with their version), the prompt version, the model id and the retrieval set.
Keep it for the whole dispute window of your market, hashed as it is written, where the bot cannot change it.
Replay from the log, never from memory, when a customer disputes an answer.

sources.label: legal-news report of the decision, 2024 BCCRT 149, 16 Feb 2024

checks.title: Cite or decline
checks.why: The ninety-day window came from nowhere. A figure, a date or a rule that the bot cannot point to is a promise nobody authorised.
do: Every answer that carries a number, a date or a policy rule quotes the page it came from, with a link.
No source found means the bot says so and hands over; it never fills the gap from training data.
Count answers with an empty sources list every day; the target is zero.
checks.code: grep -c '"sources": \[\]' answers.jsonl    # answers with no citation: want 0

sources.label: legal-news report of the decision, 2024 BCCRT 149, 16 Feb 2024

checks.title: One source of truth, stated in writing
checks.why: The tribunal found no reason a customer should know that one section of the website is accurate and another is not. Precedence has to be yours, written down, before a dispute tests it.
do: The policy page is canonical; the bot's answer is derived from it and says so in its footer.
When they disagree, the page wins and the bot is corrected inside a set time; log every correction.
Put the precedence statement in the terms the customer accepts, and in the bot's own first message.

sources.label: legal-news report of the decision, 2024 BCCRT 149, 16 Feb 2024

checks.title: A named owner and a deadline
checks.why: Disputed answers that sit in a queue become claims. A person, a replay and a reply inside a fixed number of days turn them back into tickets.
do: Route every disputed answer to a named owner with the replay attached; the deadline is in days, not 'soon'.
Track the count and the time to reply as a release metric, alongside accuracy.

sources.label: AI Incident Database, incident 639 (the chatbot's answer, Nov 2022)

checks.title: Rehearse the dispute
checks.why: A process that has never been run is a process that does not exist. The airline found out in front of a tribunal.
do: Take one real wrong answer from last month, run the replay, the source check and the reply, and time it end to end.
If any step needs a person to search a chat channel for a screenshot, fix the log first.

sources.label: legal-news report of the decision, 2024 BCCRT 149, 16 Feb 2024

checklists.title: Runaway-agent checklist
checklists.subtitle: One null value, over 15,000 reasoning calls in under an hour, a $50,000 bill; five controls that stop the loop
checklists.intro: One corrupted null value broke a ledger agent's formatting tool. It tried to brute-force a fix: more than 15,000 reasoning calls in under an hour, about $50,000 of cloud spend, and database locks that halted live transactions. Nothing capped the calls, the cost or the failures, and every retry re-sent the whole history as billable input. Five controls.

checks.title: A daily budget per agent identity
checks.why: The incident report's first control: cost-cap thresholds at the service-ID and project level. One key per agent, one budget per key; when it trips the agent stops, not the finance team.
do: Give every agent its own API key or service identity; never a shared team key.
Set a hard daily spend per identity at the provider or gateway, and a soft alert at half.
A tripped budget stops the agent and pages a person; it never raises itself.
checks.code:
agent: ledger-reconcile   identity: svc-ledger-agent   # its own key, nobody else's
daily_budget_usd: 50      # hard stop at the gateway; soft alert at 25

sources.label: threat-intelligence special report, AI risk and resilience in 2026, case study 6 (Sep 2026)

checks.title: A circuit breaker on consecutive failures
checks.why: The loop was the agent retrying its own fix. The report asks for automated financial circuit breakers that halt an agent after a set number of consecutive task failures.
do: Count failures per task, not per session; three in a row ends the run and files the task for a human.
Treat a tool error, a schema failure and an empty result as failures; a retry is not progress.
Log the last failing input with the task so the fix starts from evidence.

sources.label: threat-intelligence special report, AI risk and resilience in 2026, case study 6 (Sep 2026)

checks.title: A step limit and a depth limit per task
checks.why: Bounded recursion is the third control in the report. A task that needs more than the limit needs a person, and the limit is what turns a runaway loop into a ticket.
do: Cap tool calls per task (25 is a sane default for a reconciliation step) and sub-task depth (2).
Make hitting the limit a normal, logged outcome, never an exception that triggers a retry.

sources.label: threat-intelligence special report, AI risk and resilience in 2026, case study 6 (Sep 2026)

checks.title: Stop re-billing the history
checks.why: Tool output re-entering the context is billed again on every call. A September 2026 study measured a session's cumulative input at 14,293 times its first call; raw history adds 21 to 36 percent to its cost.
do: Summarise tool output before it re-enters the context; keep the raw result in a store read by reference.
Put a ceiling on context growth per task and on prompt size per call; measure input tokens per call, not only per session.

sources.label: Persistent Billable State: Denial-of-Wallet Attacks and Defenses in Tool-Calling LLM Agents, arXiv 2609.28585 (23 Sep 2026)

checks.title: Watch the cost curve, not the total
checks.why: A loop shows up as calls per minute and input tokens per call climbing together, long before the invoice; the report's observability control would have caught this in minutes.
do: Alert when calls per minute per identity and input tokens per call rise together for a few calls.
Rate-limit each identity at the gateway so a loop degrades instead of spiking.
Rehearse it: break a tool in staging and confirm the breaker, the budget and the alert fire.

sources.label: threat-intelligence special report, AI risk and resilience in 2026, case study 6 (Sep 2026)

checklists.title: Agent budget checklist
checklists.subtitle: A launch price that doubles on 1 December 2026, and the five numbers to set before it does
checklists.intro: A frontier model went on sale on 13 October 2026 at two dollars per million input tokens and ten per million output, for seven weeks. From 1 December the same tokens cost four and twenty. Output is five times input and includes the reasoning nobody reads. A pilot priced on the launch rate meets a December invoice at twice the price. Five checks.

checks.title: Budget at the list price
checks.why: The discount has an end date; the budget line does not. A cost model built on the launch rate is wrong by a factor of two from the first of December.
do: Put the list price in the cost model today, with the discount's end date on the ticket that owns the line.
Set the spend alert at the list price now, so the alarm is tested while the bill is still small.
checks.code:
price_per_million: {input: 4.00, output: 20.00, cached: 0.20}   # list price
alert_usd_per_day: 120   # list-price projection, from today

sources.label: trade-press report of the launch pricing, 13 Oct 2026

checks.title: An output ceiling per route
checks.why: Agents are output machines, and output costs five times input. A request cap written when the ceiling was sixty-four thousand tokens does nothing against a million-token task.
do: Size max output tokens to the job, per route, and log every request that hits the ceiling.
A million-token task is a batch job with its own approval, at half the standard rate.
Count ceiling hits every day; a rising count is a prompt problem before it is a budget problem.

sources.label: trade-press report of the launch pricing, 13 Oct 2026 (the 64,000-token ceiling raised to a million)
the full price table, 14 Oct 2026 (batch at half the standard rate)

checks.title: Cache hit rate on the dashboard
checks.why: Cached input is ninety-five percent off: at the list price, twenty cents per million against four dollars. The order of the prompt decides the bill more than the model does.
do: Stable content first: system prompt, tool schemas, reference documents; the user's turn last.
Put the cache hit rate per route next to latency and error rate; a falling rate pages someone before the invoice does.
Treat a prompt change that breaks the cache as a cost regression in review.

sources.label: the full price table, 14 Oct 2026 (cached input $0.10 now, $0.20 from 1 December)

checks.title: Thinking tokens are output
checks.why: The output rate includes the model's reasoning; the published price table says so in as many words. The answer on screen is a fraction of what was billed.
do: Log output tokens per task, split into visible answer and reasoning, and watch the ratio per route.
Set the reasoning effort per route; the cheapest setting that passes the eval is the default.

sources.label: the full price table, 14 Oct 2026 (output prices include thinking tokens)

checks.title: Rehearse 1 December
checks.why: A price step with a known date is the easiest incident to prepare for. The launch rate runs to 30 November 2026 and the list rate applies from 1 December; both dates were published on launch day.
do: Run one day of traffic through the cost model at the list price, compare it with the alert thresholds, and name who approves the line after the step.
